n: Later, back in Galilee, Jesus shows himself again to his disciples by the Sea of Tiberias. John now tells how it happened.

f.g: on this wise = in this way.

n: Seven disciples are together: Peter, Thomas, Nathanael from Cana, James and John (the sons of Zebedee), and two others.
Peter announces he’s going fishing, and the others join him. They work all night and catch nothing — just like the night before Jesus first called Peter.
At dawn Jesus stands on the beach, but the disciples don’t recognize him.

f.w: knew not that it was Jesus

n: He calls out affectionately, “Children, do you have any fish?” They answer, “No.”

f.g: meat = food; here, fish to eat.

n: He tells them to cast the net on the right side of the boat. They do — and the net is so full they can’t haul it in. Obeying his word brings abundance where their own effort failed.

f.w: Cast the net on the right side of the ship

n: The beloved disciple recognizes him first: “It is the Lord!” Impetuous Peter throws on his outer garment and jumps into the water to reach Jesus.

f.w: girt his fisher's coat unto him
f.g: He tied on his outer garment; “naked” here means stripped down to work clothes.

f.w: did cast himself into the sea

n: The others follow in the boat, about a hundred yards from shore, dragging the net full of fish.

f.g: A cubit was about 18 inches, so roughly 100 yards (90 meters).

n: On shore they find a charcoal fire with fish cooking on it and bread. Jesus has already prepared breakfast for them.

f.g: The only other charcoal fire in John is where Peter denied Jesus — the scene is set for his restoration.

n: Jesus asks them to bring some of the fish they’ve just caught. He includes their effort in the meal.

f.g: The Lord invites our contribution, even when he could supply everything.

n: Peter drags the net ashore — 153 large fish — and the net hasn’t torn. Many have seen the large catch as a symbol of the great harvest of souls the apostles would gather.

f.w: an hundred and fifty and three
f.g: A precise eyewitness count; ancient and modern readers have proposed many symbolic meanings, none certain.

f.w: yet was not the net broken

n: Jesus says, “Come and eat breakfast.” No one dares ask who he is — they know it is the Lord.

f.g: dine = eat a meal; here the morning meal.

n: Jesus takes the bread and gives it to them, and the fish too — echoing the feeding of the five thousand by the same lake.
John notes this is the third time Jesus appeared to the disciples as a group after his resurrection.

After breakfast Jesus asks Peter, “Do you love me more than these?” — more than the other disciples do, or perhaps more than the boats and fish of his old life. Peter says yes. Jesus replies, “Feed my lambs.”

f.w: lovest thou me more than these?

n: A second time Jesus asks if Peter loves him, and Peter says yes. Jesus says, “Tend my sheep.”

f.g: Greek here is poimainō — shepherd, tend, care for — a slightly different verb than in verses 15 and 17.

n: A third time Jesus asks, and Peter is hurt. He answers, “Lord, you know everything; you know I love you.” Jesus says again, “Feed my sheep.” Three questions mirror three denials — a gentle, complete restoration.

f.g: In the first two questions Jesus uses agapaō; Peter answers with phileō. The third time Jesus uses Peter’s word. Many see significance in the shift, though the words overlap in meaning.

n: Jesus then foretells Peter’s future: when young, he dressed himself and went where he pleased; when old, he will stretch out his hands, and others will bind him and take him where he would not choose to go.

f.w: thou shalt stretch forth thy hands
f.g: Early Christian tradition holds that Peter was crucified in Rome.
girded = dressed oneself, tied one’s belt.

n: John explains that Jesus was indicating the kind of death by which Peter would glorify God. Then Jesus tells him, “Follow me” — the same call he first heard by this lake.

f.w: by what death he should glorify God

n: Peter turns and sees the beloved disciple following — the one who leaned on Jesus at the Last Supper and asked who would betray him.

f.w: which also leaned on his breast at supper

n: Peter asks, “Lord, what about him?”

f.g: A natural question — but it shifts attention from Peter’s own calling.

n: Jesus answers: if he wants this disciple to remain until he returns, that’s not Peter’s concern. “You follow me.” Each disciple has their own path.

f.w: If I will that he tarry till I come
f.g: tarry = remain. Latter-day revelation teaches that John asked for and received power to remain on earth and bring souls to Christ until the Second Coming.

n: A rumor spread among believers that this disciple wouldn’t die. John corrects it: Jesus didn’t say that, only “If I want him to remain…” Latter-day Saints understand that John was translated — changed so as not to taste death until Christ’s return.
The author identifies himself as this disciple, the one who testifies of these things and wrote them down. Others add, “we know his testimony is true.”
John closes by saying that Jesus did so much more that if it were all written down, the world couldn’t hold the books. Christ’s life and works are beyond full telling.

f.w: the world itself could not contain the books
